title: Growing Strides to a Point
statement:
You stand at position 0 on an endless number line. You make moves numbered 1, 2, 3, … and move number k is exactly k units long. For each move you choose freely whether it goes left or right.

Return the smallest number of moves after which you stand exactly on target. If target is 0, the answer is 0.

examples.why: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 overshoots by 2. Turning move 1 around gives −1 + 2 + 3 = 4. Two moves reach at most 3.
Three moves reach 6 and four reach 10, but both overshoot by an odd amount, and flipping a move changes the total by an even amount. Five moves reach 15, overshoot 10, flip move 5.
1 + 2 + 3 lands on 6 with no flip needed.

hints: Left and right are symmetric, so only |target| matters. Try always moving right first: where do you end up after k moves?
After k moves to the right you are at S = 1 + 2 + … + k. Turning move m around subtracts 2m. Which overshoots S − target can you fix by turning moves around?
Any even overshoot 2d can be fixed, because some subset of 1 … k adds up to exactly d. An odd one never can. So find the first k with S ≥ target and S − target even.

explain.intuition:
Mirror the problem so the target is not negative. Now imagine all moves go right; after k moves you stand at S = k(k + 1) / 2. Flipping one move of length m to the left moves the end point by exactly 2m, so any set of flips moves it by an even amount. That means the overshoot S − target must be even, and it must not be negative.

Those two conditions are also enough. If the overshoot is 2d, you need some moves whose lengths add up to d, and d ≤ S / 2. The numbers 1 … k can be picked to make every sum from 0 to S, so such a set always exists. So the answer is the first k where S reaches the target and the overshoot is even, and that happens within at most two extra moves after S first reaches it.
steps: Grow k and the running sum S until S ≥ target.
While S − target is odd, take one more move: k++, S += k.
pitfalls: Stopping at the first k with S ≥ target. For 2 that gives 2 moves (sum 3, overshoot 1), but an odd overshoot can never be fixed.
Trying a greedy left/right choice per move. The moves interact; reason about the final sum and its parity instead.
Forgetting the negative side: the answer for -x is the same as for x.

solutions.title: Grow the sum, then fix parity
solutions.idea: Add moves until the sum reaches the target, then keep adding until the overshoot is even.

solutions.title: Jump to the first k with the quadratic formula
solutions.idea: Solve k(k + 1) / 2 ≥ t directly with a square root, then add at most two moves for parity.

followups: Return the actual list of directions, not just the count.
What if move k has length 2k − 1 instead? Which part of the argument changes?
